name: Market Socialism
summary: Market socialism holds that the means of production should be socially owned, by the public or by the workers who use them, while goods, services and usually capital goods are exchanged in competitive markets. Its theorists reject both capitalist ownership, with its unearned property income and concentrated wealth, and Soviet-style central planning, which they regard as inefficient and authoritarian. Most modern designs pair self-managed or publicly owned firms with public banks or public control over new investment, and aim at greater equality, workplace democracy and political democracy.
scope: The theoretical family as defined by its main designers: Lange's 1936-38 competitive-socialism model, Nove's feasible socialism, Roemer's coupon socialism and Bardhan and Roemer's bank-centric model, Miller's cooperative market socialism, and above all Schweickart's Economic Democracy, with Mill as forerunner and Yugoslav workers' self-management (1950 Basic Law, Tito) as its main historical experiment. Where the state-owned (Lange, Roemer, Nove) and cooperative (Mill, Schweickart, Yugoslav) strands differ, answers are 0 or low. China's and Vietnam's socialist market economies and Proudhonian mutualism are excluded; outside economics most answers are low-confidence inferences.

keyFigures.name: Oskar Lange
keyFigures.role: Designed the 1930s model of socialism in which a planning board sets prices by trial and error, answering Mises and Hayek.

keyFigures.name: David Schweickart
keyFigures.role: Author of Economic Democracy, the worker-self-managed market socialism with socially controlled investment.

keyFigures.name: John Roemer
keyFigures.role: Proposed coupon socialism, in which every citizen holds equal non-transferable shares in firms.

sources.title: Economic Democracy: A Worthy Socialism That Would Really Work (Science & Society 56:1, 1992)
sources.author: David Schweickart
sources.usedFor: Three features of the model (self-managed firms, markets, social control of investment via capital-assets tax and public banks); rejection of central planning; political democracy presupposed; interest unnecessary; labour not a commodity; alienation; legislatures setting product and technology standards; lessons from Yugoslavia and Mondragon.

sources.title: Economic Democracy
sources.author: David Schweickart / Global Justice Center
sources.usedFor: Short statement of the model: capital as social property paying a tax, workers' council electing management, prices set by supply and demand, per-capita regional allocation of investment favouring employment.

sources.title: Principles of Political Economy, Book IV, Chapter VII: On the Probable Futurity of the Labouring Classes
sources.author: John Stuart Mill
sources.usedFor: Workers' associations owning capital collectively with elected managers; defence of competition; peaceful, gradual supersession of wage labour; equal rights for women.

sources.title: Workers Manage Factories in Yugoslavia (1950)
sources.author: Josip Broz Tito
sources.usedFor: 'Factories for the workers'; state ownership as the lowest form of social ownership; bureaucracy as enemy of socialism; withering away of the state.

sources.title: Basic Law on Management of State Economic Enterprises and Higher Economic Associations by the Workers' Collectives (excerpt, 1950)
sources.author: Federal People's Republic of Yugoslavia
sources.usedFor: Elected and recallable workers' councils and management boards running enterprises in the name of the community.

sources.title: Speech at the First Congress of Workers' Councils (1957)
sources.author: Josip Broz Tito
sources.usedFor: Workers' councils dealing with market and enterprise economics; pay linked to productivity; critique of centralised management.

sources.title: Oskar Lange's Lectures on the Economic Operation of a Socialist Society (introduction)
sources.author: Tadeusz Kowalik, Contributions to Political Economy 6 (1987)
sources.usedFor: Lange's 1938 study and his later drift toward a mixed public/private market economy.

sources.title: Oskar Lange's Economics and the Socialist Economy (MPRA 111344)
sources.author: Luiz Gomes
sources.usedFor: Lange's model: Central Planning Board setting accounting prices by trial and error, free choice of consumption and occupation, planners setting accumulation; material incentives; enterprise self-management; gradual separation of economic management from the state.

sources.title: Socialism (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
sources.author: Gilabert and O'Neill, SEP
sources.usedFor: Market socialism section: Schweickart's economic democracy, Roemer's coupon socialism (no inherited wealth), critiques of central planning, socialist aims (equality, democracy, self-realisation), transition strategies.

sources.title: Review of John Roemer, A Future for Socialism
sources.author: Mises Review (David Gordon)
sources.usedFor: Roemer's stated aims (equality of opportunity for self-realisation, political influence and status), publicly controlled banks, large state role in directing investment, scepticism of all-labour-managed economies.

sources.title: Feasible Socialism? (review of Nove, The Economics of Feasible Socialism Revisited)
sources.author: Stephen Louw, Transformation 21 (1993)
sources.usedFor: Nove's mix of state, socialised, co-operative and limited private enterprise; planning against market externalities; health and education outside the market.

sources.title: Socialism: Feasible and Viable? (review of Nove)
sources.author: Wlodzimierz Brus, New Left Review I/153
sources.usedFor: Nove's and Brus's rejection of Marxist plans to abolish money and markets; nationalisation not identical with socialisation.

sources.author: Wikipedia

sources.author: Mel Bienenfeld, Against the Current 2003 (marxists.org)

sources.title: Market Socialism: A Case for Rejuvenation (working paper abstract)
sources.author: Pranab Bardhan and John E. Roemer
sources.usedFor: Competitive markets needed for efficiency but full private ownership not needed; bank-centric monitoring of firms.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Nove places health and education outside market relations, and Schweickart lists hospitals and schools among the free public goods funded from the public investment fund.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: In worker-run firms workers take the residual, so a wage floor matters little to the model itself; adherents are split between wage floors for remaining hired labour and the view that the issue falls away.

public-ownership.rationale: Most designs keep productive capital in social hands: Schweickart calls the means of production the collective property of society, Lange's enterprises are state-owned, and Nove wants public ownership to dominate with industries like electricity outside workforce control; Roemer and the cooperative strand care less about classic state utilities.

property-fundamental.rationale: Private ownership of productive property is removed or limited in every model, so private property cannot be a near-inviolable right, although personal property and savings remain.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Schweickart's socialism has no commitment to laissez-faire: it allows price controls in monopolised industries and lets legislatures prohibit products and set technology standards, and Nove calls for planning against unpriced externalities.

cut-welfare.rationale: Schweickart's public sector acts as employer of last resort and the schemes aim at equal shares and a social dividend, so welfare cuts contradict the egalitarian design.

worker-ownership.rationale: Worker cooperatives are the usual form in the models. Schweickart's workers control but rent capital from society and Mill expected collective ownership by workers, though state-owned variants exist, so agree not strongly.

strong-leader.rationale: Models stress democratic control at the firm and public level and critique authoritarian planning, so a leader bypassing gridlock is opposed.

state-harmful.rationale: The models give the state or public agencies a central role in owning capital and steering investment, which rules out treating the state as inherently harmful.

decide-locally.rationale: Schweickart passes investment funds down to regions and communities per capita, but the capital tax and national priorities stay central, so the balance is split.

nation-first.rationale: The model keeps capital at home but takes no stand on putting national interest above global cooperation.

revolution-justified.rationale: Mill expected change without violence and Schweickart's transition runs through an elected government, yet Schweickart writes within a Marxist revolutionary frame and the Yugoslav system came out of a revolution, so adherents are split.

central-planning.rationale: Schweickart writes that central planning both concentrates power in an authoritarian way and is inefficient, and Roemer concedes the Soviet model is dead; markets for goods are a defining commitment.

socialized-markets.rationale: The family is defined by combining social ownership of firms with competitive markets; Schweickart's model is explicitly a worker-self-managed market socialism and Bardhan and Roemer argue markets need not rest on full private ownership.

land-value-tax.rationale: Mill favoured taxing unearned land rent but replacing most other taxes with it is not a market-socialist position.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Roemer's coupons cannot be bequeathed, so no inherited wealth in firms is allowed, and Mill favoured limiting inheritance; heavy inheritance taxes fit that aim.

basic-income.rationale: Corneo and Roemer designs distribute a social dividend from public ownership of capital to citizens, which functions as a basic income.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: The model favours fair trade and domestic capital but no tariff policy is specified.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Schweickart makes social control of new investment one of his model's three basic features, with legislatures deciding which sectors to encourage through grants from a capital-tax fund, and Roemer gives the state a large role in steering investment.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Roemer spreads share ownership equally among citizens, but productive property is socially held rather than owned by small owners, and Nove and Schweickart only tolerate a limited small private sector; split.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Nove and Brus reject the Marxist hope of abolishing money and markets, and every model keeps money; the cooperative strand does replace wages with shares of net revenue, so the full statement is rejected but not strongly.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: State-recognized employer and worker bodies setting wages and prices together is not part of the models; prices come from markets.

one-party-rule.rationale: Schweickart's model presupposes multiparty representative democracy with civil liberties, distinguishing itself from pre-1989 Yugoslavia.

democracy-best.rationale: Schweickart presupposes constitutional, representative government with civil liberties for all and argues that people trusted to elect presidents can elect their bosses; the modern theorists treat political democracy as part of the project.

direct-votes.rationale: Workplace and public votes are central, but direct legislation by citizens is not part of the models.

natural-rulers.rationale: Mill and market socialists reject inherited or natural privilege; the egalitarian one-person-one-vote model of firms rules this out.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Market socialists often reject the Marxist theory of history; Schweickart sidesteps Marx's deeper concepts, though some such as Wolff come from Marxism, so adherents are split.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Roemer frames the socialist aim as equality of opportunity for self-realisation, welfare and political influence, and Schweickart lets each firm's workers vote for unequal income shares, so equal outcomes are not the target.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Mill defends competition but also cooperation; the models use self-interest through markets without treating it as a moral good.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: Environmental concern appears but no stated stance on intrinsic value.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: The models seek to reorganize industrial economies, not reject them.

restore-past-order.rationale: The models aim to build a new economic order, not restore an old one.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Nove and Schweickart argue largely on feasibility and efficiency, but they also appeal to democratic and egalitarian principle, so the answer is split.

direct-action.rationale: Models rely on elections, reforms and cooperatives; direct action over parliaments is not endorsed.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Markets, firms and specialised management remain in all models, so the division of labour is not abolished.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Distribution follows market incomes and profit shares, with only a social dividend for equality, not the need principle of full communism.

production-for-use.rationale: Firms still produce for sale in competitive markets and profits are shared, so production is not organised around use alone.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Some market socialists (Wolff, Roemer) adopt Marxist exploitation theory, others hold that capital ownership skews markets without calling profit exploitation; the field is split.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Market socialists present democratic alternatives to dictatorial planning, so reject class dictatorship.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: Schweickart blames capitalism for many structural ills but the inevitable-imperialism thesis is not part of the models.

taxation-theft.rationale: The models rely on the capital assets tax and taxation to fund a social dividend, so taxation is legitimate.

harm-principle.rationale: Mill's liberal framework includes it, and modern adherents are broadly liberal, but the economic models do not address it.

exit-over-voice.rationale: The models stress democratic voice in firms and public life over exit as the main check.

state-as-business.rationale: The state is viewed as a democratic instrument of public investment, not a firm with customers.

total-state.rationale: Opposed by the central idea of decentralised markets and worker self-management.

bound-labor.rationale: Mill and the models aim to end dependent labour and give workers control over their work.

single-common-good.rationale: Models rely on markets and democratic bargaining among interests rather than a single reasoned common good.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Mill wanted workers' associations with managers elected and removable by the workers, the 1950 Yugoslav law put enterprises under elected workers' councils, and Schweickart's firms are run one person, one vote.

economic-freedom.rationale: Mill and market socialists value markets but do not hold that political freedom requires private ownership; the opposite thesis that economic democracy is needed is argued instead.

ban-interest.rationale: Schweickart sees no need to pay interest on savings and his later reforms abolish it, but he also accepts moderate interest from savings cooperatives, and Lange's and Roemer's designs keep a price for capital, so the strands are split.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Market socialists see the state as a democratic instrument of investment, not purely a class tool; Marxian strands (Wolff) partly differ.

night-watchman-state.rationale: The models require a state for public investment, taxation and market rules.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Equal votes in firms and Mill's equality of terms in associations rest on equal standing.

socialism-one-country.rationale: Models such as Yugoslavia's and Schweickart's national designs presume socialism can exist in one country.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: The models aim at democratic markets, not a strengthened state under siege.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Not directly stated, but democratic control of firms and public investment rests on consent; Mill is a liberal.

trade-surplus.rationale: Schweickart favours fair trade but no export-surplus goal.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Libertarian non-aggression is not endorsed, since the models rely on taxation and public ownership.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: Wage workers' dependence on employers is seen as a form of domination; Mill and Schweickart aim to end hired dependence by workers controlling firms.

vanguard-party.rationale: The models rely on democratic firms and elected governments, not a revolutionary party.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Schweickart attributes poverty to capitalism's structure, not population growth.

constituent-assembly.rationale: The model is an economic design compatible with any constitutional route, so the issue is outside it.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Market socialists justify ownership by social benefit, putting firms under worker or public control, though their markets keep strong property rights within firms.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: Market socialists criticize central planning and Soviet-type economies, but whether to call them state capitalist or flawed socialist varies among adherents.

space-expansion.rationale: No stance in the literature and no obvious lean from its principles; adherents are split.

common-currency.rationale: Economic model silent on monetary union; Schweickart-style designs favour regulated trade, so split.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: The models are about institutions, and the sources do not take a side on historical causation; split.

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: Egalitarian but the economic models do not address representation rules; split.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Schweickart's model favours regulated fair trade with markets, not an autarkic closed bloc.

moral-incentives.rationale: Lange held that once the socialist economy matures, material interest in enterprise profitability should drive work, and Schweickart ties workers' income to the firm's net revenue.

patriotic-education.rationale: Indifferent: the model concerns ownership of firms; adherents are split on patriotic schooling and the model does not address it.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Aims to remove the large inequalities that make such duties necessary, though a duty to help others is not rejected; adherents split.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: An economic model with no settled stance on culture; adherents split.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: Market socialists accept world markets and disagree on whether they are exploitative; split.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: Condemns both dictatorships, but many resist calling them equivalent; split.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Models stress that institutions should suit local conditions, but adherents are divided on civilizational claims; split.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: The theorists reject both capitalist ownership and Soviet central planning, presenting their model as a third form between them.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Market socialism rests on democratic enterprise control and political pluralism, so suppressing opposition contradicts it.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Schweickart extends democracy into every workplace and uses public investment hearings and referenda, and the Yugoslav system put enterprises under elected councils.

assisted-dying.rationale: Adherents are split on this and the economic model is silent on it.

alienated-labor.rationale: Schweickart says worker self-management exists to break the commodity character of labour-power and the alienation that goes with it, and the SEP lists self-realising work as a core socialist aim.

religious-dress-in-state.rationale: Adherents are split and the economic model is silent on it.

social-market-economy.rationale: Market socialism accepts markets and welfare but rejects capitalist ownership, so adherents would only partly endorse a capitalist-style social market.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Foreign policy is outside the economic model and adherents are split.

reification.rationale: Marxist-influenced market socialists such as Wolff may accept the critique, but the family's core claim is that markets are a useful coordinating device, so adherents are split.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Market socialists argue that concentrated private wealth lets a dominant class skew markets and politics, and Schweickart criticises outcomes that enrich the 1 percent.

power-sharing-divided-societies.rationale: The model is silent on constitutional design for divided societies, and its adherents have no common position on consociationalism versus majority rule.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Market socialists seek a more equal economy through institutional design and public provision, not reliance on voluntary charity, which they see as inadequate to structural inequality.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Schweickart pays no interest or dividends to private holders, and labour in his firms shares the net revenue; Roemer instead spreads property income equally through coupons, so the principle is endorsed but not always as reward for work alone.

socialism-needs-workers-power.rationale: Tito presented workers' management of factories as the core of real socialism against Soviet bureaucratic centralism, and Schweickart makes workers' control of firms basic.

municipal-property.rationale: In Mill's and Schweickart's models the firm is controlled by its own workers and capital is held by society, not owned by the municipality.

capital-controls.rationale: Public control of investment is central, but this concerns domestic allocation; adherents are split on cross-border limits.

collective-bargaining.rationale: Where firms are not worker-owned, social ownership aims at fairer pay; unions and bargaining are generally supported, though worker self-management reduces the need.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Market socialism works through democratic institutions and public enterprises, not revolutionary destruction of the state.

religions-one-truth.rationale: An economic model with no stated view on religion; adherents are typically secular and pluralist, so this is a weak inference.

keep-nuclear-weapons.rationale: The model is silent on defence and adherents split between pacifist and mainstream-left positions; neutral inference.

workers-own-party.rationale: Adherents are split between working-class parties and broad social-democratic parties; the model itself is silent.

immigrants-learn-language.rationale: The model is silent on immigration and language, and adherents are split; neutral inference.

women-suffrage.rationale: The models rest on democratic participation on equal terms, so equal voting and office rights are taken for granted.

defend-planned-state.rationale: Market socialism is defined against comprehensive central planning, so adherents would not treat defending a planned economy as their cause, though many sympathise with socially owned property.

simple-living.rationale: The model concerns ownership and markets, not personal consumption; adherents are split, as it accepts market consumption.

distribution-by-process.rationale: Schweickart and Roemer object to unearned property income and concentrated wealth, so an unequal result is not made just by voluntary steps alone.

material-over-identity.rationale: Adherents' main concern is economic ownership, but Mill and Schweickart also stress equal rights; the sources give no direct answer.

market-under-party-rule.rationale: Lange and Yugoslavia combined markets with party-led socialism, while Schweickart presupposes political democracy; strands are split.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: Schweickart's public sector acts as employer of last resort and the schemes aim at equal shares and a social dividend, so welfare cuts contradict the egalitarian design. (Carried over from cut-welfare, "Welfare programs create dependency and should be cut.", with the value reversed, 2026-11-11.)

missingStatements.text: New investment should be funded by a tax on business capital and allocated through public banks rather than by private savers and shareholders.
missingStatements.rationale: Social control of investment through a capital-assets tax and public banks is one of the three defining features of Schweickart's model, and Roemer and Bardhan also route capital through publicly controlled banks.
missingStatements.declined: Statement bank frozen on 2026-10-22, before the people audits: no new statements are added.

missingStatements.text: Firms should be managed by their own workers on a one-person, one-vote basis.
missingStatements.rationale: Worker self-management is the core of Mill's associations, the 1950 Yugoslav law and Economic Democracy; workplace-democracy covers it loosely but this states the governance rule.
missingStatements.declined: Statement bank frozen on 2026-10-22, before the people audits: no new statements are added.

notes: Strands differ mainly on who holds firms (state or public agencies in Lange, Roemer and Nove; workers in Mill, Schweickart and Yugoslavia) and on interest, which Schweickart would largely abolish but other designs keep. Yugoslav self-management operated under one-party rule, while the modern theorists presuppose multiparty democracy; the profile follows the modern theorists on political questions. Lange later moved toward a mixed public-private economy. Primary books by Lange, Nove, Roemer and Miller could not be opened online, so their positions are cited through scholarly reviews and summaries.
